newsitem.title: FRANCE: Le Pen says French better off under left.
newsitem.headline: Le Pen says French better off under left.

text.p: Extreme-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said on Sunday the left's recent victory in France was a better result than if the ousted centre-right had returned to power.

Heaping scorn on defeated premier Alain Juppe, and backhanded praise on new Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, Le Pen told a rally he preferred the Socialists because of the centre-right's concerted attacks on the National Front.
"Mr Jospin is less brutal than the man who thought he was comfortable in his boots for life," Le Pen said, citing a defiant line of Juppe, who lost a general election on June 1.

The left's victory was less serious because its voters would prevent it going down the road of "euro-capitalism" favoured by President Jacques Chirac, he said. Le Pen staunchly opposes a planned single European currency or closer European integration.
Le Pen has a score to settle with Juppe, who last year called the anti-immigration leader "deeply, almost viscerally racist, antisemitic and xenophobic".

During the campaign, Le Pen urged his party's supporters to go all out to defeat Juppe. The National Front scored its biggest result for a parliamentary election, with 15 percent of the vote, giving it one seat in the National Assembly.
The Socialists and allies won the biggest share of seats, with the Communists holding the balance of power on 38 seats.

"The left remains a utopian and incapable adversary, but I would say I loathe their opponents even more because the UDF and RPR (centre-right parties) are united in demonising the National Front," Le Pen said.
He was speaking in one of the four towns in southern France controlled by the National Front.
In another, the Mediterranean port city of Toulon, an anti-racist group said on Sunday it would defy a National Front ban and go ahead with a planned Bastille Day liberty festival.
Fode Sylla, president of SOS-Racisme, said mayor Jean-Marie Le Chevallier of the National Front had no grounds for banning the long-planned open-air event.
Le Chevallier, who initially cited a threat to public order, told Reuters he had given prior permission for a jazz festival on the same site and there was no reason to occupy it.

The National Front, which advocates sending home three million immigrants and limiting jobs, social services and public housing to native-born French people, has long been at loggerheads with SOS-Racisme.
